claim: Fronto-temporal dementia (FTD) is the second most prevalent form of early onset dementia.
source: Fronto-temporal dementia (FTD) is the second most prevalent form of early onset dementia (Bang et al., 2015; Cairns et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bang et al., 2015 and Cairns et al., 2007

claim: The misfolding and aggregation of proteins such as tau, TDP-43, FUS, or ubiquitin-positive proteins encompass nearly all cases of FTD.
source: The misfolding and aggregation of proteins such as tau, TDP-43, FUS, or ubiquitin-positive proteins encompass nearly all cases of FTD (Seelaar et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Seelaar et al., 2011

claim: FTD clinical phenotype includes behavioural, executive, and language dysfunction without primary amnesia.
source: FTD clinical phenotype includes behavioural, executive, and language dysfunction without primary amnesia.
evidence: Based on established clinical characterization of FTD

claim: The initial clinical manifestation of the disease characterizes FTD cases into three common variants: the behavioural (BV) and two distinct forms of primary progressive aphasias, the semantic (SV) and the progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA).
source: The initial clinical manifestation of the disease characterizes FTD cases into three common variants: the behavioural (BV) and two distinct forms of primary progressive aphasias, the semantic (SV) and the progressive non-fluent aphasia (PNFA).
evidence: Based on established clinical classification of FTD variants

claim: White matter (WM) is much involved in the pathophysiology of FTD.
source: While FTD has long been considered a grey-matter (GM) disease, recent advance in diffusion MRI (dMRI) research has revealed that white matter (WM) is also much involved in the pathophysiology of the disease (Zhang et al., 2009; McKenna et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2009 and McKenna et al., 2021

claim: GM atrophy is typically observed in the insula in all FTD variants.
source: GM atrophy is typically observed in the insula (Muhtadie et al., 2021) (all variants), the bilateral anterior cingulate and frontal lobe (BV) (Lanata and Miller, 2016), left anterior temporal lobe (SV) (Williams et al., 2005), and left premotor and inferior frontal cortex (PNFA) (McMillan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muhtadie et al., 2021

claim: GM atrophy is typically observed in the bilateral anterior cingulate and frontal lobe in BV.
source: GM atrophy is typically observed in the insula (Muhtadie et al., 2021) (all variants), the bilateral anterior cingulate and frontal lobe (BV) (Lanata and Miller, 2016), left anterior temporal lobe (SV) (Williams et al., 2005), and left premotor and inferior frontal cortex (PNFA) (McMillan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lanata and Miller, 2016

claim: GM atrophy is typically observed in the left anterior temporal lobe in SV.
source: GM atrophy is typically observed in the insula (Muhtadie et al., 2021) (all variants), the bilateral anterior cingulate and frontal lobe (BV) (Lanata and Miller, 2016), left anterior temporal lobe (SV) (Williams et al., 2005), and left premotor and inferior frontal cortex (PNFA) (McMillan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al., 2005

claim: GM atrophy is typically observed in the left premotor and inferior frontal cortex in PNFA.
source: GM atrophy is typically observed in the insula (Muhtadie et al., 2021) (all variants), the bilateral anterior cingulate and frontal lobe (BV) (Lanata and Miller, 2016), left anterior temporal lobe (SV) (Williams et al., 2005), and left premotor and inferior frontal cortex (PNFA) (McMillan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to McMillan et al., 2004

claim: Widespread WM abnormalities have been observed in the uncinate fasciculus, superior frontal, inferior frontal and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi, the corpus callosum and the cingulum bundle in FTD.
source: Widespread WM abnormalities have been observed in the uncinate fasciculus, superior frontal, inferior frontal and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi, the corpus callosum and the cingulum bundle, with a large overlap amongst participants; see Greaves and Rohrer, 2019; Meeter et al., 2017; Rohrer et al., 2010, for recent reviews of MRI findings in FTD.
evidence: Supported by citations to Greaves and Rohrer, 2019; Meeter et al., 2017; Rohrer et al., 2010

claim: In some mutation carriers, WM changes are detectable up to 30 years before symptoms onset.
source: In some mutation carriers, WM changes are detectable up to 30 years before symptoms onset (Jiskoot et al., 2018), strengthening the importance of considering WM alteration as part of the pathophysiology of FTD.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiskoot et al., 2018

claim: Alteration from GM may propagate to WM via Wallerian degeneration or retrograde degeneration.
source: Alteration from GM may propagate to WM and, reciprocally, WM damage may propagate to GM via Wallerian degeneration or retrograde degeneration (Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2019; Villain et al., 2008; Villain et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2019; Villain et al., 2008; Villain et al., 2010

claim: WM damage may propagate to GM via Wallerian degeneration or retrograde degeneration.
source: Alteration from GM may propagate to WM and, reciprocally, WM damage may propagate to GM via Wallerian degeneration or retrograde degeneration (Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2019; Villain et al., 2008; Villain et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Metzler-Baddeley et al., 2019; Villain et al., 2008; Villain et al., 2010

claim: Studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to discrete aspects of cognition in BV and SD including disinhibition.
source: Nonetheless, a number of studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to discrete aspects of cognition in BV and SD including disinhibition (Piguet et al., 2011), moral reasoning (Strikwerda-Brown et al., 2021), and WM changes over time (Lam et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piguet et al., 2011

claim: Studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to moral reasoning in BV and SD.
source: Nonetheless, a number of studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to discrete aspects of cognition in BV and SD including disinhibition (Piguet et al., 2011), moral reasoning (Strikwerda-Brown et al., 2021), and WM changes over time (Lam et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strikwerda-Brown et al., 2021

claim: Studies have related WM changes over time to cognition in BV and SD.
source: Nonetheless, a number of studies have related both GM and WM atrophy to discrete aspects of cognition in BV and SD including disinhibition (Piguet et al., 2011), moral reasoning (Strikwerda-Brown et al., 2021), and WM changes over time (Lam et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lam et al., 2014

claim: Semantic symptoms were mainly dependent on short-range WM fibre disruption in FTD.
source: We found that semantic symptoms were mainly dependent on short-range WM fibre disruption, while damage to long-range WM fibres was preferentially associated to executive dysfunction with the GM contribution to cognition being predominant for local processing.
evidence: Based on the study's findings from tract-specific analyses

claim: Damage to long-range WM fibres was preferentially associated to executive dysfunction in FTD.
source: We found that semantic symptoms were mainly dependent on short-range WM fibre disruption, while damage to long-range WM fibres was preferentially associated to executive dysfunction with the GM contribution to cognition being predominant for local processing.
evidence: Based on the study's findings from tract-specific analyses

claim: GM contribution to cognition is predominant for local processing in FTD.
source: We found that semantic symptoms were mainly dependent on short-range WM fibre disruption, while damage to long-range WM fibres was preferentially associated to executive dysfunction with the GM contribution to cognition being predominant for local processing.
evidence: Based on the study's findings from tract-specific analyses

claim: Large-scale WM tracts are particularly vulnerable to vascular disease.
source: As large-scale WM tracts, which are particularly vulnerable to vascular disease, were highly associated with executive dysfunction, our findings highlight the importance of controlling for risk factors associated with deep WM disease, such as vascular risk factors, in patients with FTD in order not to potentiate underlying executive dysfunction.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about WM vulnerability to vascular disease

claim: All FTD variants had extensive WM impairments compared to normal controls after correction for age, sex, and intracranial volume.
source: Variants of FTD all had extensive WM impairments compared to normal controls after correction for age, sex, and intracranial volume (ICV) (Figure 1).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis results shown in Figure 1

claim: Reduced FC could be observed in large associative fibres including the uncinate fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum, and corpus callosum irrespective of the FTD variant.
source: Irrespective of the variant, reduced FC (Figure 2a–c; upper panels) could be observed in large associative fibres including the uncinate fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus and the superior longitudinal fasciculus, cingulum, and corpus callosum.
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 2a-c

claim: BV presented with variant-specific differences in the bilateral anterior and medial part of the frontal cortex and lateral orbitofrontal WM.
source: Despite a large common network, variant-specific differences could be noted in the bilateral anterior and medial part of the frontal cortex and lateral orbitofrontal WM for BV (Figure 2a), while PNFA presented with reduced FC in the caudal part (precentral gyrus/supplementary motor area [SMA]) of the left frontal cortex (Figure 2b) and SV showed a left predominant FC reduction in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 2c).
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 2a

claim: PNFA presented with reduced FC in the caudal part (precentral gyrus/supplementary motor area) of the left frontal cortex.
source: Despite a large common network, variant-specific differences could be noted in the bilateral anterior and medial part of the frontal cortex and lateral orbitofrontal WM for BV (Figure 2a), while PNFA presented with reduced FC in the caudal part (precentral gyrus/supplementary motor area [SMA]) of the left frontal cortex (Figure 2b) and SV showed a left predominant FC reduction in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 2c).
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 2b

claim: SV showed a left predominant FC reduction in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
source: Despite a large common network, variant-specific differences could be noted in the bilateral anterior and medial part of the frontal cortex and lateral orbitofrontal WM for BV (Figure 2a), while PNFA presented with reduced FC in the caudal part (precentral gyrus/supplementary motor area [SMA]) of the left frontal cortex (Figure 2b) and SV showed a left predominant FC reduction in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 2c).
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 2c

claim: Reduced FD patterns were similar to those observed for FC although with a lower spatial extent.
source: Reduced FD patterns (Figure 2a–c; lower panels) were similar to those observed for FC although with a lower spatial extent.
evidence: Based on comparison of FD and FC results shown in Figure 2a-c

claim: BV had the largest reduction in bilateral insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity compared to normal controls.
source: Compared to normal controls, BV (Figure 2d) had the largest reduction in bilateral insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity, followed by bilateral reduction in thalamo-frontal (rostral middle frontal) connectivity.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2d

claim: BV had bilateral reduction in thalamo-frontal (rostral middle frontal) connectivity compared to normal controls.
source: Compared to normal controls, BV (Figure 2d) had the largest reduction in bilateral insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity, followed by bilateral reduction in thalamo-frontal (rostral middle frontal) connectivity.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2d

claim: For PNFA, the largest reduction was observed in insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity in the left hemisphere only.
source: For PNFA (Figure 2e), the largest reduction was also observed in insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity but in the left hemisphere only, followed by precentral – middle frontal connectivity impairment.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2e

claim: PNFA showed precentral – middle frontal connectivity impairment.
source: For PNFA (Figure 2e), the largest reduction was also observed in insula – inferior frontal cortex (pars opercularis and triangularis) connectivity but in the left hemisphere only, followed by precentral – middle frontal connectivity impairment.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2e

claim: For SV, the largest reduction occurred in the left hemisphere between the thalamus and the temporal cortex (superior and middle).
source: For SV (Figure 2f), the largest reduction occurred in the left hemisphere between the thalamus and the temporal cortex (superior and middle), but also between the lateral orbitofrontal and superior frontal cortex, followed by intra-temporal connectivity reduction.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2f

claim: SV showed reduction between the lateral orbitofrontal and superior frontal cortex.
source: For SV (Figure 2f), the largest reduction occurred in the left hemisphere between the thalamus and the temporal cortex (superior and middle), but also between the lateral orbitofrontal and superior frontal cortex, followed by intra-temporal connectivity reduction.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2f

claim: SV showed intra-temporal connectivity reduction.
source: For SV (Figure 2f), the largest reduction occurred in the left hemisphere between the thalamus and the temporal cortex (superior and middle), but also between the lateral orbitofrontal and superior frontal cortex, followed by intra-temporal connectivity reduction.
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 2f

claim: BV had a widespread reduction in bilateral GM volume with the strongest effect seen in the insula, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
source: BV (Figure 3a) had a widespread reduction in bilateral GM volume with the strongest effect seen in the insula, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior) while PNFA (Figure 3b) had a left predominant atrophy in the premotor part of the frontal cortex, the insula and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior), and SV (Figure 3c) had a bilateral (but left predominant) atrophy of the whole temporal lobes and to a lesser extend insula atrophy.
evidence: Based on VBM analysis results shown in Figure 3a

claim: PNFA had a left predominant atrophy in the premotor part of the frontal cortex, the insula and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
source: BV (Figure 3a) had a widespread reduction in bilateral GM volume with the strongest effect seen in the insula, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior) while PNFA (Figure 3b) had a left predominant atrophy in the premotor part of the frontal cortex, the insula and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior), and SV (Figure 3c) had a bilateral (but left predominant) atrophy of the whole temporal lobes and to a lesser extend insula atrophy.
evidence: Based on VBM analysis results shown in Figure 3b

claim: SV had a bilateral (but left predominant) atrophy of the whole temporal lobes and to a lesser extent insula atrophy.
source: BV (Figure 3a) had a widespread reduction in bilateral GM volume with the strongest effect seen in the insula, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior) while PNFA (Figure 3b) had a left predominant atrophy in the premotor part of the frontal cortex, the insula and prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior), and SV (Figure 3c) had a bilateral (but left predominant) atrophy of the whole temporal lobes and to a lesser extend insula atrophy.
evidence: Based on VBM analysis results shown in Figure 3c

claim: The three FTD variants share overlapping GM atrophy in the insula.
source: Taken together (Figure 3d), the three variants share overlapping GM atrophy in the insula, while BV and SV share atrophy in the temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex, and PNFA and BV share atrophy in the left prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
evidence: Based on overlay analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: BV and SV share atrophy in the temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex.
source: Taken together (Figure 3d), the three variants share overlapping GM atrophy in the insula, while BV and SV share atrophy in the temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex, and PNFA and BV share atrophy in the left prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
evidence: Based on overlay analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: PNFA and BV share atrophy in the left prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
source: Taken together (Figure 3d), the three variants share overlapping GM atrophy in the insula, while BV and SV share atrophy in the temporal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex, and PNFA and BV share atrophy in the left prefrontal cortex (middle and inferior).
evidence: Based on overlay analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: A strong relationship was found between GM atrophy and reduced FC and FD for the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and superior longitudinal fasciculus independently of the seed location.
source: Independently of the seed location, a strong relationship was found between GM atrophy and reduced FC and FD for the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus, and superior longitudinal fasciculus.
evidence: Based on seed-based analysis results shown in Figure 4

claim: GM volume for the BV orbitofrontal seed was associated with the inferior part of the precentral cortex.
source: GM volume for the BV orbitofrontal seed (Figure 4a) was also associated with the inferior part of the precentral cortex, PNFA premotor seed (Figure 4b) with the precentral WM fibres, and SV inferior temporal seed with impairment in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
evidence: Based on seed-based analysis results shown in Figure 4a

claim: GM volume for the PNFA premotor seed was associated with the precentral WM fibres.
source: GM volume for the BV orbitofrontal seed (Figure 4a) was also associated with the inferior part of the precentral cortex, PNFA premotor seed (Figure 4b) with the precentral WM fibres, and SV inferior temporal seed with impairment in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
evidence: Based on seed-based analysis results shown in Figure 4b

claim: GM volume for the SV inferior temporal seed was associated with impairment in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
source: GM volume for the BV orbitofrontal seed (Figure 4a) was also associated with the inferior part of the precentral cortex, PNFA premotor seed (Figure 4b) with the precentral WM fibres, and SV inferior temporal seed with impairment in the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
evidence: Based on seed-based analysis results shown in Figure 4c

claim: A three common factor model provides a satisfactory explanation for the variation in the cognitive test data.
source: As highlighted earlier, our three factor model failed to reject the null hypothesis suggesting that this model provides a satisfactory explanation for the variation in this data.
evidence: Based on statistical testing of the factor model (approximate chi-squared test; p < 0.42)

claim: The first cognitive factor was mainly related to semantic processing and comprised naming, category fluency, and verbal learning scores (delayed and immediate recall).
source: According to the loadings of this analysis, the first factor (Factor 1) was mainly related to semantic processing and comprised naming, category fluency, and verbal learning scores (delayed and immediate recall).
evidence: Based on factor loadings shown in Figure 5a

claim: The second cognitive factor was mainly related to executive processing and comprised digit span, trail making, and letter fluency scores.
source: The second factor (Factor 2) was mainly related to executive processing and comprised digit span, trail making, and letter fluency scores.
evidence: Based on factor loadings shown in Figure 5a

claim: The third cognitive factor was only related to verbal fluency (category and letter).
source: The third factor (Factor 3) was only related to verbal fluency (category and letter).
evidence: Based on factor loadings shown in Figure 5a

claim: SV patients had on average a lower semantic factor score compared to BV (p = 0.034) and PNFA (p < 0.001).
source: Although SV patients had on average a lower semantic factor score compared to BV (p = 0.034) and PNFA (p < 0.001) and a higher executive factor score (p < 0.001; vs. BV and PNFA), a large within-group variability can be noted for all factors (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of factor scores shown in Figure 5b

claim: SV patients had a higher executive factor score (p < 0.001; vs. BV and PNFA).
source: Although SV patients had on average a lower semantic factor score compared to BV (p = 0.034) and PNFA (p < 0.001) and a higher executive factor score (p < 0.001; vs. BV and PNFA), a large within-group variability can be noted for all factors (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on statistical comparison of factor scores shown in Figure 5b

claim: The semantic factor was significantly associated to FC in the uncinate fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, and the inferior longitudinal fasciculus.
source: After correction for age, sex, ICV, and multiple comparisons, the first (semantic) factor was significantly associated to FC in the uncinate fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, and the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (Figure 5d; upper panel).
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 5d

claim: The semantic factor was associated to reduced connectivity between the left GM temporal regions amongst themselves but also with the supramarginal, lateral orbitofrontal gyrus, and with the thalamus.
source: The semantic factor was also associated to reduced connectivity between the left GM temporal regions amongst themselves but also with the supramarginal, lateral orbitofrontal gyrus, and with the thalamus (Figure 5c).
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 5c

claim: The executive factor was significantly associated with a reduced FC in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, superior corona radiata, body of the corpus callosum, inferior frontal and precentral WM, and in fibres corresponding to the aslant tract.
source: The second (executive) factor was significantly associated with a reduced FC in the superior longitudinal fasciculus, superior corona radiata, body of the corpus callosum, inferior frontal and precentral WM, and in fibres corresponding to the aslant tract (Figure 5d; lower panel).
evidence: Based on fixel-based analysis results shown in Figure 5d

claim: Reduced structural connectivity for the executive factor was predominantly observed between the left superior frontal gyrus and other GM frontal regions (pars orbitalis, pars triangularis, lateral orbitofrontal, rostral middle frontal, and precentral gyrus).
source: Reduced structural connectivity was predominantly observed between the left superior frontal gyrus and other GM frontal regions (pars orbitalis, pars triangularis, lateral orbitofrontal, rostral middle frontal, and precentral gyrus), accompanied by a reduced connectivity between left superior frontal gyrus and other cortices (insula, the superior temporal gyrus, and between the inferior parietal cortex) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 5c

claim: Reduced structural connectivity for the executive factor was accompanied by a reduced connectivity between left superior frontal gyrus and other cortices (insula, the superior temporal gyrus, and between the inferior parietal cortex).
source: Reduced structural connectivity was predominantly observed between the left superior frontal gyrus and other GM frontal regions (pars orbitalis, pars triangularis, lateral orbitofrontal, rostral middle frontal, and precentral gyrus), accompanied by a reduced connectivity between left superior frontal gyrus and other cortices (insula, the superior temporal gyrus, and between the inferior parietal cortex) (Figure 5c).
evidence: Based on structural connectivity analysis results shown in Figure 5c

claim: FD yielded similar spatial relationships to FC for cognitive factors.
source: Although not shown in the figure, FD yielded similar spatial relationships than FC.
evidence: Based on comparison of FD and FC analysis results

claim: No significant relationship could be found between the third factor (verbal fluency) and FC, FD, or structural connectivity.
source: No significant relationship could be found between the third factor (verbal fluency) and FC, FD, or structural connectivity (not shown).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the third factor

claim: GM volume and FC better explained the variance for the first cognitive factor (semantic) (39.2% and 32.2%, respectively) than FD (12.7%).
source: After correcting for age, sex, and ICV, GM volume and FC better explained the variance for the first cognitive factor (39.2% and 32.2%, respectively) than FD (12.7%) (Figure 6a; right panels).
evidence: Based on variance explained analysis shown in Figure 6a

claim: For the second cognitive factor (executive), FC explains the variance better (31.7%) than GM (18.5%) and FD (18.9%).
source: On the other hand, for the second factor, FC explains the variance better (31.7 %) than GM (18.5%) and FD (18.9%) (Figure 6b; right panels).
evidence: Based on variance explained analysis shown in Figure 6b

claim: For most connections, GM, FD, and FC could predict cognition when used as single predictors.
source: The comparisons of all the selected connection standardized estimates revealed that, for most connections, GM, FD, and FC could predict the cognition (Figure 6c; left panel).
evidence: Based on standardized estimates shown in Figure 6c left panel

claim: When GM, FD, and FC were included together in the same general linear models, the contribution of the WM was reduced but not for all connections.
source: Importantly, when included together in the same general linear models (GLM) (Figure 6c; right panel), the contribution of the WM was reduced but not for all connections.
evidence: Based on partial estimates shown in Figure 6c right panel

claim: A positive relationship was found between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length for FD (p = 0.006).
source: We then tested the relationship between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length and found a positive relationship for FD (Figure 6d; left panel, p = 0.006) and a trend level negative relationship for GM (Figure 6d; right panel, p = 0.058), but not for FC (Figure 6d middle panel, p = 0.94).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6d

claim: A trend level negative relationship was found between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length for GM (p = 0.058).
source: We then tested the relationship between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length and found a positive relationship for FD (Figure 6d; left panel, p = 0.006) and a trend level negative relationship for GM (Figure 6d; right panel, p = 0.058), but not for FC (Figure 6d middle panel, p = 0.94).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6d

claim: No relationship was found between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length for FC (p = 0.94).
source: We then tested the relationship between the standardized estimates and the average fibre length and found a positive relationship for FD (Figure 6d; left panel, p = 0.006) and a trend level negative relationship for GM (Figure 6d; right panel, p = 0.058), but not for FC (Figure 6d middle panel, p = 0.94).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6d

claim: All FTD cases had FD or FC abnormalities across a large WM network connecting the frontal and temporal cortices.
source: We found that, although regional differences in WM properties were observed in all variants, all FTD cases had FD or FC abnormalities across a large WM network connecting the frontal and temporal cortices.
evidence: Based on the study's fixel-based analysis results

claim: WM abnormalities were linked to patterns of GM atrophy and cognitive decline across FTD variants.
source: Furthermore, these WM abnormalities were linked to patterns of GM atrophy and cognitive decline across FTD variants.
evidence: Based on the study's correlation analyses

claim: The differential contributions of WM and GM on cognition depended on the length of WM fibre.
source: The differential contributions of WM and GM on cognition depended on the length of WM fibre.
evidence: Based on the study's tract-specific analysis results

claim: The study identified a large network (uncinate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, cingulum, and corpus callosum) of WM impairment being shared across FTD variants.
source: Our study identified a large network (uncinate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, cingulum, and corpus callosum) of WM impairment being shared across FTD variants, extending findings from previous reports (Agosta et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on the study's fixel-based analysis results and supported by citation to Agosta et al., 2015

claim: SV has additional impairments in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.
source: Also in line with previous literature, we found SV to have additional impairments in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (Acosta-Cabronero et al., 2011; Agosta et al., 2010; Galantucci et al., 2011; Matsuo et al., 2008; Whitwell et al., 2010), BV in the frontal cortex (Agosta et al., 2012; Mahoney et al., 2014; Piguet et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2009), and PNFA in SMA WM fibres (Agosta et al., 2015; Mahoney et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on the study's results and supported by citations to Acosta-Cabronero et al., 2011; Agosta et al., 2010; Galantucci et al., 2011; Matsuo et al., 2008; Whitwell et al., 2010

claim: BV has additional impairments in the frontal cortex.
source: Also in line with previous literature, we found SV to have additional impairments in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (Acosta-Cabronero et al., 2011; Agosta et al., 2010; Galantucci et al., 2011; Matsuo et al., 2008; Whitwell et al., 2010), BV in the frontal cortex (Agosta et al., 2012; Mahoney et al., 2014; Piguet et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2009), and PNFA in SMA WM fibres (Agosta et al., 2015; Mahoney et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on the study's results and supported by citations to Agosta et al., 2012; Mahoney et al., 2014; Piguet et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2009

claim: PNFA has additional impairments in SMA WM fibres.
source: Also in line with previous literature, we found SV to have additional impairments in the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (Acosta-Cabronero et al., 2011; Agosta et al., 2010; Galantucci et al., 2011; Matsuo et al., 2008; Whitwell et al., 2010), BV in the frontal cortex (Agosta et al., 2012; Mahoney et al., 2014; Piguet et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2009), and PNFA in SMA WM fibres (Agosta et al., 2015; Mahoney et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on the study's results and supported by citations to Agosta et al., 2015; Mahoney et al., 2013

claim: One of the largest reductions in structural connectivity was between thalamo-frontal regions in FTD.
source: In addition, we found that one of the largest reductions in structural connectivity was between thalamo-frontal regions, supporting the finding that thalamic atrophy is a prominent feature of FTD (Diehl-Schmid et al., 2019) and that it is common across episodic and genetic mutation (Bocchetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on the study's structural connectivity results and supported by citations to Diehl-Schmid et al., 2019 and Bocchetta et al., 2018

claim: Thalamic atrophy is a prominent feature of FTD.
source: In addition, we found that one of the largest reductions in structural connectivity was between thalamo-frontal regions, supporting the finding that thalamic atrophy is a prominent feature of FTD (Diehl-Schmid et al., 2019) and that it is common across episodic and genetic mutation (Bocchetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Diehl-Schmid et al., 2019

claim: Thalamic atrophy is common across episodic and genetic mutation in FTD.
source: In addition, we found that one of the largest reductions in structural connectivity was between thalamo-frontal regions, supporting the finding that thalamic atrophy is a prominent feature of FTD (Diehl-Schmid et al., 2019) and that it is common across episodic and genetic mutation (Bocchetta et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bocchetta et al., 2018

claim: A common semantic factor explained the variance of scores in the immediate and delayed verbal memory test, picture naming, and categorical verbal fluency across the FTD spectrum.
source: Across the FTD spectrum, we found that a common semantic factor explained the variance of scores in the immediate and delayed verbal memory test, picture naming, and categorical verbal fluency.
evidence: Based on the study's factor analysis results

claim: Semantic information contributes significantly in phonological lexical activation.
source: This is in line with several studies showing poorer lexical retrieval of semantically degraded words vs. semantically intact words (Jefferies et al., 2004; Knott et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 1994), suggesting that semantic information contributes significantly in (phonological) lexical activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jefferies et al., 2004; Knott et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 1994

claim: Studies show poorer lexical retrieval of semantically degraded words vs. semantically intact words.
source: This is in line with several studies showing poorer lexical retrieval of semantically degraded words vs. semantically intact words (Jefferies et al., 2004; Knott et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 1994), suggesting that semantic information contributes significantly in (phonological) lexical activation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Jefferies et al., 2004; Knott et al., 2000; Patterson et al., 1994

claim: TMT measures multiple executive functions, including attention, processing speed, and set-shifting.

TMT measures multiple executive functions, including attention, processing speed, set-shifting, and digit span (forward and backward), and is typically used as an attentional/working memory measure, while phonemic verbal fluency contains both a working memory/executive and a language component.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TMT

claim: Digit span (forward and backward) is typically used as an attentional/working memory measure.
source: The second cognitive factor (executive) explained the variance of scores in the modified trail making processing time, digit span (forward and backward), and phonemic, but not categorical, verbal fluency. TMT measures multiple executive functions, including attention, processing speed, set-shifting, and digit span (forward and backward), and is typically used as an attentional/working memory measure, while phonemic verbal fluency contains both a working memory/executive and a language component.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about digit span

claim: Phonemic verbal fluency contains both a working memory/executive and a language component.

source: A third factor grouped the two verbal fluency tests together, however this factor only partly explains the variance of each test as they also weighed on semantic processing (for category fluency) and executive functioning (letter fluency), supporting the dual nature of the verbal fluency test (Whiteside et al., 2016) even in non-demented individuals.

claim: Evidence exists for the relationship between semantic deficits and WM impairment in the left uncinate fasciculus, inferior longitudinal fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, across all FTD variants.

claim: The uncinate fasciculus has been associated with semantic processing in many studies.

claim: Brain stimulation studies and post-mortem fibre dissection studies have linked the ventral subcomponent of the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus to semantic processing.

claim: Prior studies led to inconsistent results regarding the involvement of the inferior longitudinal fasciculus to semantic processing.

claim: The connectivity between the left inferior temporal cortex and the thalamus may be involved in semantic processing.

claim: The findings support the hub model for semantic processing where the anterior temporal pole represents a unique trans-modal hub receiving and assembling information from different modality specificity brain regions via specific WM connections.
source: In general, our findings support the so-called hub model for the semantic processing where the anterior temporal pole represents a unique trans-modal hub receiving and assembling information from different modality specificity brain regions via specific WM connections (Patterson et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on the study's findings and supported by citation to Patterson et al., 2007

claim: It was proposed that graded deficit in semantic processing is dependent on the WM fasciculi connecting the anterior temporal lobe to the cortex, where the uncinate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus would convey either social, verbal, or visual semantic processing, respectively.
source: Interestingly, it was also proposed (Ralph et al., 2017) that graded deficit in semantic processing is dependent on the WM fasciculi connecting the anterior temporal lobe to the cortex, where the uncinate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus would convey either social, verbal, or visual semantic processing, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ralph et al., 2017

claim: The hub hypothesis for semantic processing could be expanded further by considering subcortical contribution to the model.

claim: The superior longitudinal fasciculus has previously been associated to processing speed.

claim: The superior longitudinal fasciculus has previously been associated to working memory.

evidence: Supported by citation to Rizio and Diaz, 2016

claim: Impairment of the corona radiata has been associated to executive dysfunction.
source: The superior longitudinal fasciculus (connecting the frontal lobe to temporal and parietal cortices) has previously been associated to processing speed (Turken et al., 2008) and working memory (Rizio and Diaz, 2016) and impairment of the corona radiata (connecting the prefrontal cortex to the basal ganglia and thalamus) has also been associated to executive dysfunction (Hua et al., 2014; Moeller et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hua et al., 2014; Moeller et al., 2015

claim: The integrity of the aslant tract correlated with the amount of distortion errors that PNFA patients made in spontaneous speech.
